summary.title: Undervalued Software Engineering Skills: Writing Well
summary.one_liner: Writing clearly and concisely is a high-leverage skill for engineers who need to influence teams beyond their immediate peers, and it can be practiced through reading, self-editing, and feedback.
takeaways: Writing becomes essential as engineering teams grow beyond face-to-face communication, to make decisions, tradeoffs and proposals durable.
Documents such as proposals, coding guidelines, runbooks, debugging guides, postmortems and even code reviews benefit from good writing.
Improving writing follows the usual skill loop: learn fundamentals, practice, get feedback, and repeat.
Recommended starting books are On Writing Well and The Sense of Style; the author also suggests re-reading and re-editing your own work and asking strong writers for feedback.
Writing well is presented as a key skill for moving from senior engineer to lead, staff or distinguished engineer roles.
summary.summary: The author, a former engineer now coaching engineers as an engineering manager, argues that writing is an undervalued skill that becomes critical as organizations grow and face-to-face communication is no longer enough. He explains which kinds of engineering artifacts benefit from clear writing and why writing is key to influencing people beyond one's immediate team. The post suggests practical steps: studying writing fundamentals in books such as On Writing Well and The Sense of Style, re-reading and editing one's own work, shortening messages, using tools like Grammarly and the Hemingway App, and seeking feedback from good writers. It ends by citing Urs Hölzle on clear writing as an engineering superpower.
